summaries.summary: Humor bridges languages, cultures, ages and demographics, while Automatic Humor Recognition is challenging due to external knowledge, humor types and differing interpretations.
Most social media research focuses on English, but non-English and code-mixed content, especially Hindi-English in India with 41% Hindi speakers and 23.2 million Twitter users, needs technologies.
The paper presents a freely available corpus of Latin-script Hindi-English code-mixed tweets manually classified as humorous or non-humorous with token-level language tags.
This section explains the techniques used in the creation and annotation of the corpus.
Python package twitterscraper extracted 10,478 tweets, from which 4161 English, 2774 Hindi and 3543 English-Hindi code-mixed tweets were identified.
The authors tried to make the corpus balanced with uniform distribution of tweets in each category for better supervised classification results.
Three university-student annotators fluent in English and Hindi spent approximately 60 hours tagging final code-mixed tweets for humor presence.
“For #WontGiveItBack to work, Dhoni needs to say `Trophy toh ghar par hi bhul aaye' ” is an example code-mixed tweet.
(For #WontGiveItBack to work, Dhoni needs to say “We forgot the trophy at home”) is the provided translation.
Na sadak na naukri bas badh rahi gundagardi #FailedCMNitish is an example code-mixed tweet.
(No roads no naukri, only hooliganism increasing #FailedCMNitish ) is the provided translation.
Subha ka bhula agar sham ko wapas ghar aa jaye then we must thank GPS technology is an example code-mixed tweet.
(If someone lost in the morning return home in the evening then we must thank GPS technology.) is the provided translation.
She : Gori hai kalaiyan pehna de mujhe hari hari chudiya He *gets green bangles* She : Not this green ya, bottle green color is an example tweet.
(She : (sings a song) My wrists are so beautiful, give me green green bangles He *gets green bangles* She : Not this green ya, bottle green color. ) is the provided translation.
Dard dilon ke kam ho jaate... twitter par agar poetries kam ho jaate is an example code-mixed tweet.
(pain in the heart will reduce...if number of poetries decreases on twitter). is the provided translation.
Annotators used hashtag and keyword searches, humor guidelines, Fleiss' Kappa agreement of 0.821, balanced classes, mixed domains and unimodal filtering to categorize tweets.
Tokens were annotated at word level with En, Hi and Ot tags, with ambiguous words resolved by context, meaning and usage.
Figure 1 illustrates annotations with tweet id, <tweet></tweet>, <word lang=“ ”></word> and <class></class> tags, and the annotated dataset is available online.
Spelling mistakes and variations were corrected, including replacing `dis' with `this' and standardizing transliterated Hindi words across the corpus.
This section describes the machine learning model trained and tested on the corpus described in the previous section.
Preprocessing tokenizes by spaces, lowercases words, removes punctuation, replaces hashtags, mentions and urls, decomposes camel-case hashtags, and stores humor as the target class.
Character level and word level features are used, with words separated by language annotation and combined into each tweet's feature vector.
Letter n-grams are language independent and efficient for code-mix texts, so trigrams occurring more than ten times in the corpus were used.
A three word window was used as a feature to incorporate contextual information for understanding sentence semantics in humor classification.
Common words in jokes, idioms and decomposed hashtags were identified and included as classification features.
Four classifiers, support vector machine, random forest, extra tree and naive bayes classifier, were tested using Chi square feature selection and Scikit-learn.
10-fold cross validation on 3543 code-mixed tweets yielded 69.3% accuracy for support vector machine with radial basis function kernel and 67.8% for extra tree classifier.
The paper describes a freely available corpus of 3453 English-Hindi code-mixed tweets, humor and language tags, features, and best accuracy of 69.3%.
Future work includes part-of-speech tags, more domains, more than two languages, transliteration issues, and comparison with merged monolingual English and Hindi tweets.
